doc.title: Greg Thomas interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 11, 2014

title: The 'Race and Jazz' series and why race is an illusion
summary: Thomas explains his All About Jazz series, race versus culture, his NYU graduate work, and how the music of Woods, Desmond and Sims kept him from racism.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: I wanted to talk about, I read this about you, under the banner of “Race and Jazz,” to shed light on the way that race has bedeviled the jazz discourse in the actual lives of jazz musicians. It’s a topic that gets written about a lot, and I’m wondering what you’re thinking about it at this point.

Well the intent of that series in All About Jazz was to, frankly to use the issue of race to point the way to culture. Because race biologically speaking is an illusion unless you’re talking about the human race. It almost sounds like a cliché but it’s true. But race certainly has — there’s a psychological and social and behavioral dimension to race that’s very real. Because if you believe, let’s take you Monk. If I make certain judgments about you based on the pigment of your skin or your height or your weight or some attribute like that, if I make certain presumptions and then treat you in a certain manner because of that, then you have to then adjust yourself based on my belief and my behavior towards you based on attributes that, in a larger sense, are immaterial and should not be the basis upon judging, or assuming certain behaviors, or assuming certain values you know. If, you know, if you have this skin pigment therefore you think or behave in a certain fashion. I mean it sounds absurd because it is. It is absurd. But I’m leading to the culture piece.
Okay, well and also you can make assumptions about, if we’re talking about musicians, where you’re going to be more likely to play in a certain way.

Oh yeah. Oh that’s true. But these days that’s usually not the case because there’s such diversity of styles within the music that it’s hard to just look at someone and say well they play such-and-such a style. That’s hard these days I’d say. But getting back to what I was saying about race and culture, so race itself as a biological reality is an illusion you know. But because race has become a part of the way people look at things, the way some people look at things and the way people then behave towards others, then that gets in the mix so you have to deal with that. I think a much better to look at human interaction, group behavior, values, traditions, practices, modes of passing down those through education, myths and rituals that are related to those things, is culture. So the issue of race is, so it’s like the third rail they say in American discussion, in American discourse. But I was willing to take the risk of dealing with that because one, I have thought about and read about these issues for decades. I did some graduate work at NYU in American Studies, a doctoral program, in which it allowed me to continue my interdisciplinary work that I started here at Hamilton. So I went into more depth in literature and anthropology and history in particular, both the subjects themselves as well as a critical body of work and thought in those areas, which has given me a really broad view of these issues. I know that personally, and this is something that I tell in the very first entry into that series, the first essay, which I called if I remember correctly, “Jazz Versus Racism.” You see the series is “Race and Jazz.” But “Jazz Versus Racism” was the title of the first piece. So my first line is jazz, help me to not become a racist, or something along that line. And it told about my time here at Hamilton where, because I was studying in depth about enslavement, the middle passage, and those details. I got angry. I mean, you know, like in the late 70s, while in high school, watching Roots. It got you angry. But, you know, really studying this stuff. So but what happened, and with Mr. Louis Farrakhan and the Nation of Islam was pretty big at the time, around the time that Jesse Jackson was running for president and that kind of thing. You know, and we’d listen to tapes here, and that kind of thing. But the thing that never allowed me to jump over the cliff and become a racist, and I don’t believe the canard that if you’re black you can’t be a racist because race is about power relations. I don’t buy that. I mean not that race isn’t about power relations, but it’s not just about that. You could have a point of view about someone based on their physical attributes — that ain’t got a damn thing to do with whether or not you have power over them. Now if you have some kind of power over them it becomes worse, which is what black people have had to deal with for a long time. But you can still have a point of view about other people based on those kind of attributes and not have that. So I don’t buy that particular argument. So I got to a point where I had to actually make a choice. Am I going to, based on this anger, based on this history, am I going to actually start to dislike white people, you know? And the thing that

didn’t allow me to make that leap was the music. Because I loved Phil Woods and his playing. Because I loved Paul Desmond. I loved Zoot Sims. And that was like a shield that protected me against falling prey to that kind of thinking, man.
